description: We are Fatesa, a team from São José do Rio Preto, Brazil. We’re working on the Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data challenge, building a tool that uses NASA Earth data to help farmers adapt to a changing climate. Our team is complete and we are not looking for new members.
summary: A web app for farmers who are switching or renewing a crop. From the field's coordinates, it reads NASA POWER (rain by month, heavy rain, drought, the rain trend over the years, heat and frost), MODIS vegetation (NDVI), SRTM terrain slope and Sentinel-2 images of the field, and asks the farmer what matters most. It turns these data into ranked crop-rotation options for the land until the next planting, always compared with what is done today. Each option explains what it matches, its gains and its risks, shows the months to watch for heat and heavy rain, and plays the field's year month by month next to NASA rainfall. After choosing, the farmer can follow the field through satellite images.  Decisions between harvests are usually made without local data. The app brings decades of NASA records to the farmer in plain language, with voice, a glossary, English and Portuguese, and a "NASA data" seal on every NASA value, so the farmer can discuss clear options with an agronomist.
details:
FATESA is a web app for farmers who are switching or renewing a crop. The farmer shares their location (GPS or the name of the town), says what is planted and what matters most to them, such as keeping the rain from washing the soil away or spending less on fertilizer. From the field's coordinates, the back end reads NASA POWER (rain by month, heavy rain, drought, the rain trend over the years, heat and frost), MODIS vegetation (NDVI), SRTM terrain slope and soil data, and applies open, documented rules: no black box. The app then shows ranked crop-rotation options for the land until the next planting, always compared with what is done today. Each option says what it matches, what the farmer gains and what can go wrong. After choosing, the farmer can follow the field through recent Sentinel-2 satellite images, and the app checks whether the plant cover matches the plan.

Benefits

The farmer sees the months to watch for heat and heavy rain, plays the field's year month by month next to NASA rainfall, compares options side by side and gets a summary to take to an agronomist.

Intended impact

Better-informed decisions between harvests, using decades of NASA records for the farmer's own field, in plain language. The goal is to help farmers protect the soil in the riskiest months and choose rotations that fit their climate and priorities.

Tools and software

Front end: TypeScript, React and Vite, built mobile-first. Back end: Python and FastAPI, with pandas, NumPy, rasterio, h5py and pyproj for the data, PostgreSQL with PostGIS, and Google Cloud Storage for processed data. Voice narration uses the browser's speech synthesis. No special hardware: it runs on a phone or a computer.

How it is creative

It turns satellite and climate data into pictures, plain words and voice. Every NASA value carries a "NASA data" seal. "Your field's year" animates the land month by month. The app switches to Portuguese and °C for Brazilian towns, and to English and °F elsewhere. A glossary explains NASA terms.

Factors we considered

Farmers with little time or technical vocabulary; use in the field on a phone; honesty about missing data (the app says "No data" instead of guessing); the limits of each dataset; and the need for an agronomist to validate any decision.
